messages.subject: Re: RSFs
messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris and Jesse,

I was able to successfully run rsf.fit and rsf.select for an individual puma using unmasked rasters (as an initial test) but I have several questions as I try to finalise the approach to the RSF analysis using ctmm:

1.     Should I use rsf.fit() or rsf.select() to determine mean() RSF parameter estimates for the population?

       I have produced one UD per individual puma using akde() and I want to calculate the mean RSF parameter estimates for the puma population at each study site. I have chosen 5 to 7 predictor variables that I think are potentially important drivers of habitat selection by pumas. I have tested both rsf.fit and rsf.select on the same data (using unmasked rasters) and it appears that only rsf.fit returns parameter estimates (for all variables included in the raster list, or specific variables if formula included), whereas rsf.select tests all combinations of predictor variables and assesses model performance rather than providing parameter estimates.

Given this, would the correct approach be just to run rsf.fit using all the predictor variables for each individual and derive mean() population level parameter estimates? If I were to run rsf.select first, I would likely end up with a different best model for each individual and hence I couldn’t calculate mean population parameter estimates if each best fit model does not contain the same predictor variables – this approach may also make comparison across study areas difficult. Is this correct?

Furthermore, below is the rsf.select output indicating that for this individual that ‘distance_to_water’ is the best performing model. This could suggest that deriving parameter estimates for the other predictor variables could be a waste of time (at least for this individual) but given I believe that my predictor variables could be important to how the population of pumas selects habitat, is it appropriate to use all predictor variables and derive the population parameter estimates? Or would you suggest a different approach?

       2.     Calculating parameter estimates for males and females at each study site

       Following the above, if I want to compare parameter estimates between the population of males and females within each study site, should I just run rsf.fit with all predictor variables and create a list of RSF outputs for males and females and calculate the mean() parameter estimates, i.e. use the same approach as for calculating the population level mean parameter estimates?

       3.       How to handle NAs / unavailable areas in rasters when running rsf.fit or rsf.select?

        When generating UDs with akde(), I removed outliers but used all other location fixes, even those falling in water due to location error. However, I did enforce hard boundaries using the ‘SP’ argument in akde() when calculating UDs.

 When I tried running rsf.fit or rsf.select on rasters that contain NA values, I received the following error message:

 Error in ctmm::rsf.fit(otook_tom, UD = otook_tom_ud, R = rsf_masked_raster_list, : NA values in sampled variables distance_to_road, distance_to_water, ruggedness, tree_cover_percent_2020, aspect.0_4, aspect.1_4, aspect.2_4, aspect.3_4 at points 81,82

 Is there an efficient way to handle sampling of NAs/unavailable areas? Is manually removing locations that fall in areas that are unavailable/NA (in my case water) the only way to deal with this? Could an argument be added to rsf.fit and rsf.select allowing the user to choose if they want sampled NAs to be automatically removed?

I also tried the offset() argument in the in rsf.fit as per below, by supplying a raster with water areas masked, in the hope that it might deal with the issue:

formula = ~ aspect + distance_to_road + distance_to_water + ruggedness + tree_cover_percent_2020 + offset(offset_raster)

but I received the following error:

Error in offset(offset_raster) : could not find function "offset".

        4.       When using a categorical variable such as aspect, does each category effectively become a separate predictor variable that risks over-parameterizing the model?

        5.       Is the sample size for the rsf models the effective sample size from akde (i.e. DOF area)?

        6.       Below is the code I used to run rsf.fit and I have the following questions re. arguments:

                                                              i.      reference – what is this actually doing? The only categorical predictor variable I am currently using is aspect, which has 5 categories as factor levels of 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, denoting flat, north, east, south, west. The reference category is automatically getting set to 4 but then 4 does not appear to be a predictor variable in the results (i.e. there are no parameter estimates provided for it – see output below). Is this correct? How do I determine the parameter estimate for the reference category? Or do I need to make 5 rasters containing binary values, i.e. one for each aspect direction?

                                                             ii.      integrator = “Riemann” – this was about 20% quicker than “MonteCarlo”, would you recommend using one over the other? I am not using many predictor variables compared to observations so Reimann could be appropriate but I don’t know how to determine if the function is smooth or spikey…(I read these are important considerations).

                                                           iii.      level.UD – I believe this uses a default value of 0.99, but as I was planning on reporting the 0.95 UD point estimate from akde(), is 0.95 the value I should use here?

                                                            iv.      error, debias, smooth & interpolate – under what circumstances should the default settings not be used?

wRSF <- ctmm::rsf.fit(otook_tom,

                                           UD = otook_tom_ud,

                                           R = rsf_raster_list,

                                           integrated = TRUE,

                                           level.UD = 0.95,

                                           trace = TRUE,

                                           standardize = TRUE,

                                           integrator = "Riemann",

                                           verbose = TRUE)

       7.       How to interpret rsf.fit output?

        Below are the summary parameter estimates from my first rsf.fit attempt. How should these be interpreted? Do positive values indicate selection and negative values avoidance? All the low and high estimates for each predictor variable cross zero, does that mean no predictor variable should be considered significant in this instance?

       8.       What does area (square kilometers) represent below, because these are not the same home range area estimates that I obtained from akde for this individual…?

We have GPS collar data for multiple pumas across multiple study areas in both North and South America and multiple kill and bed sites for each puma. Study areas are exposed to differing combinations of external factors (i.e. wolves, bears, humans). So, we are more interested in what is happening at a population level per study area rather than at the individual puma level. I understand we can derive population level parameters from RSFs by placing individual estimates in a list and calculating mean().

> > >
> > > Habitat selection per seasonal home range:

> > > - Calculate akdes per season
> > > - Create separate RSFs for winter and summer for each individual, using seasonal akdes and location data (I think NDVI will be the only time dependent variable being used in the RSFS, so we should use mean summer NDVI for summer RSF, and use mean winter NDVI for winter RSF)
> > > - Calculate population level/study area RSF parameter estimates using mean()

> > > Habitat selection for bed and kill sites per season:

> > > - Calculate population level/study area RSF parameter estimates using mean()

> > > 6. winter only bed sites
> > > 7. summer locations

Or can I just create a single seasonal akde from the beginning, despite a large time gap between the same season across multiple years?
> > >
> > > 3. If I want to assess seasonal habitat selection, do I need to first create a seasonal akde (i.e. Winter kill site selection should only be assessed relative to winter akde, not the entire akde across all seasons)?

messages.subject: Re: RSFs
messages.body_plain:
Hi Luke,
rsf.select() with verbose=TRUE returns the list of candidate models, and you can run summary() on any model in that list to see their parameter estimates, with the first model being the selected model.
In general, you do not want to feed non-selected models into mean() because unsupported features can cause numerical errors in the covariance matrix, and the covariance matrix is used in the meta-analysis weights. Unsupported features also aren't really going to be contributing very much information to the population estimates, anyhow.
mean() can handle different individuals having different selected parameters.
As a simple rule I would use rsf.select() before mean(), but the second model here probably wouldn't hurt anything because its within an AIC/parameter.
I can add an argument to drop NA location fixes - I'll add that to the to-do list.
Regarding the formula error, do you have the stats package loaded? Maybe try stats::offset(). I'll look into my code - I probably have set the formula environment incorrectly.
Yes, in any regression context, a categorical variable with N categories is expanded into N-1 indicator variables with N-1 regression parameters. Therefore, you might consider more parsimonious candidate models where some of those categories are combined in a reasonable way, and rsf.select() will not do this for you.
Yes, that is the approximate correction for the autocorrelation - using the autocorrelated Gaussian effective sample size rather than the nominal sample size: https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/2041-210X.14025
i. In any regression context, N categories is expanded into N-1 indicator variables that are relative to the reference category, which must be sampled. Here your predictors are 0 relative to 4, 1 relative to 4, 2 relative to 4, and 3 relative to 4. You can only ever estimate a categorical effect relative to a different category (or some combination thereof).
ii. If you have finely sampled raster data and aren't using a non-stationary model, then it should be faster to use Riemann.
iii. level.UD is only used for conventional non-integrated analyses, which is not recommended.
iv. With Monte-Carlo integration, you might adjust error for computational speed when setting up an analysis, otherwise you probably wouldn't touch those in normal use.
Yes and yes, but its better to use model selection to help tease out the significant parameters as unsupported parameters can potentially corrupt the covariance matrix estimate with numerical error.
The model-fit summary contains Gaussian area estimates and Gaussian RMS speed estimates. The akde() and speed() estimates are non-parametric: https://ctmm-initiative.github.io/ctmm/reference/summary.ctmm.html
Best,
Chris

> Hi Luke,
> rsf.select() with verbose=TRUE returns the list of candidate models, and you can run summary() on any model in that list to see their parameter estimates, with the first model being the selected model.
> In general, you do not want to feed non-selected models into mean() because unsupported features can cause numerical errors in the covariance matrix, and the covariance matrix is used in the meta-analysis weights. Unsupported features also aren't really going to be contributing very much information to the population estimates, anyhow.
> mean() can handle different individuals having different selected parameters.
> As a simple rule I would use rsf.select() before mean(), but the second model here probably wouldn't hurt anything because its within an AIC/parameter.
> I can add an argument to drop NA location fixes - I'll add that to the to-do list.
> Regarding the formula error, do you have the stats package loaded? Maybe try stats::offset(). I'll look into my code - I probably have set the formula environment incorrectly.
> Yes, in any regression context, a categorical variable with N categories is expanded into N-1 indicator variables with N-1 regression parameters. Therefore, you might consider more parsimonious candidate models where some of those categories are combined in a reasonable way, and rsf.select() will not do this for you.
> Yes, that is the approximate correction for the autocorrelation - using the autocorrelated Gaussian effective sample size rather than the nominal sample size: https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/2041-210X.14025
> i. In any regression context, N categories is expanded into N-1 indicator variables that are relative to the reference category, which must be sampled. Here your predictors are 0 relative to 4, 1 relative to 4, 2 relative to 4, and 3 relative to 4. You can only ever estimate a categorical effect relative to a different category (or some combination thereof).
> ii. If you have finely sampled raster data and aren't using a non-stationary model, then it should be faster to use Riemann.
> iii. level.UD is only used for conventional non-integrated analyses, which is not recommended.
> iv. With Monte-Carlo integration, you might adjust error for computational speed when setting up an analysis, otherwise you probably wouldn't touch those in normal use.
> Yes and yes, but its better to use model selection to help tease out the significant parameters as unsupported parameters can potentially corrupt the covariance matrix estimate with numerical error.
> The model-fit summary contains Gaussian area estimates and Gaussian RMS speed estimates. The akde() and speed() estimates are non-parametric: https://ctmm-initiative.github.io/ctmm/reference/summary.ctmm.html
> Best,
> Chris

Hi Soham,

The automated choice is pretty good now (in the development branch), and that dt should be reported in a message. It should be the smallest interval adjusted to an integer fraction of the median interval. And if the dataset is small enough, this should automatically switch over to the exact algorithm.

Only in a large dataset with extreme variability in the sampling intervals should the automated choice need to be adjusted.

Best,
Chris

messages.body_plain:
Hi Luke,

I would only select one model. The problem with model averaging is how do you average the covariances. If the averaged models share predictors or have colinear predictors, then the conventional way of averaging covariances as if the models are independent will underestimate uncertainties.
I don't have a reference for this, specifically. The existing RSF meta-analysis work that I know just assumed the same parameters for each individual, but did recognize that some could be missing and didn't propose anything for that IIRC.
The offset variable does need to be a boolean (1|0). Having to call stats::offset will be fixed in the next push.
I need to fix the documentation, standardize was called rescale previously. This will only happen with no formula argument or a trivial formula argument.
Standardizing the predictors is generally good for numerical stability and optimization in regression analysis.
Best,
Chris

messages.subject: Re: Optimal Weighing
messages.body_plain:
Hi Soham,

The exact algorithm has a computational cost of O(n^3), where n is the number of data points. This is very slow for tens of thousands of location fixes.

The fast algorithm has a computational cost of O(N log(N)), where N is the number of grid points. This is reasonably fast for millions of grid points. However, if you have 1 Hz data and 1 year gaps, then the automated grid intervals will be 1 second and will span the gaps, which can make for an extremely large N. Eventually, you will run out of memory this way.

Best,
Chris

messages.subject: Re: Optimal Weighing
messages.body_plain:
Hi Soham,

With error=FALSE, you should be able to change the pch plot argument to something other than a circle, or the type argument, etc.. Otherwise, this is automated according to the density of points for visibility.

If you run dt.plot() you can see the time intervals in your data, and if some so small that the animal does not move very far in that time span compared to the location error, then you either need a location error model or to thin out the small sampling intervals.

Without HDOP values or calibration data, I would set a prior of around 20-30 meter error for GPS data, as in the vignette example: https://ctmm-initiative.github.io/ctmm/articles/error.html

It is best to setup the error model before outlier detection, otherwise the default error values are being used (e.g., 10 meters), which is likely okay anyhow.

Best,
Chris

Hi Luke,

I need to code offset() to not be tested by rsf.select(). I'll have that working by this weekend.

A good test of the outputs of rsf.fit() is by plotting the suitability() raster.

Yes, with any non-trivial formula, internal standardization is turned off in rsf.fit() for safety. Standardization would change the meaning of the offset raster, because it would no longer be (0|1). I can code the offset raster to be ignored by standardization, though.

I haven't coded offsets to automatically remove data points. The easiest way is probably to use extract() on the offset raster.

The dataset that goes into rsf.fit() needs to be the same as what went into the akde() weights, or the weights and data points will not match.

At some point I will have the location errors propagated into rsf.fit() but until then, I will add an na.rm argument.

Best,
Chris

messages.subject: Re: Optimal Weighing
messages.body_plain:
Hi Soham,

I don't see any big outliers if those maximum speeds are realistic for your species.

You can/should assign an error model to all the individuals.

When fitting your movement model + location error model, your error estimate increased from the ~20 meter prior to a 40-52 meter posterior estimate. That's taking a couple of hectares from the error-less home-range area estimate (and almost half the diffusion rate estimate) and assigning that to the location error model. Without calibration data and/or more structure in the error model (such as from HDOPs), it's hard to say if this is an appropriate division of the variance. Are there no other columns in the data (DOP, number of satellites, anything)? Are there any data from the same model collar that you can use for calibration (sleeping or dead individuals, testing)? If not, this sounds like the best that you can do.

Best,
Chris

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for that Chris! :)

1. I assume 'standardize' also ignores categorical predictors such as 'aspect' ...?
Yeah, coding the offset raster to be ignored by standardization will be useful so that standardization doesn't need to be manually performed by users when their formula doesn't include interaction terms.

2. You said: 'I haven't coded offsets to automatically remove data points. The easiest way is probably to use extract() on the offset raster.'
Sorry if I am being a bit slow, but at what stage of the process do you suggest this be performed to account for animal location fixes falling in unavailable areas such as water (i.e. NA values)? Should this be done before running akde() so I can identify and remove offending points before generating UDs, and therefore rsf.fit() can be run with rasters that contain NA areas, because there won't be any locations falling within NA areas to throw an error...?

Given you said: 'The dataset that goes into rsf.fit() needs to be the same as what went into the akde() weights, or the weights and data points will not match.'  I can't see how locations within NA/unavailable areas could be removed after the UD has been created by akde(), if I want to run rsf.fit().

3. I assume predictor rasters should contain NA areas (if necessary) so these areas are not being assessed by rsf.fit() as available habitat for parameter estimation...? Or will 'offset' appropriately deal with this issue?

I ran the suitability raster as per your suggestion with the following, which worked well. Just putting here in case it is useful to others.

suitability_raster <- ctmm::suitability(data = otook_tom, #Telemetry object
                                                                  CTMM = wRSF_select[[1]], #Specific rsf.fit() model generated when running rsf.select()
                                                                  R = rsf_raster_list, #List of rasters used in RSF fitting and includes raster for selected model
                                                                  level = 0.95,
                                                                  grid = otook_tom_ud) #UD for individual generated by akde()

plot(suitability_raster[[2]]) #Plot estimate
plot(otook_tom, suitability_raster[[2]]) #Include animal locations

Thanks again,
Luke.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Luke,

At present you would need to remove the points before akde(), but I will try to have something easier working by this weekend. I am teaching at the UBC AniMove workshop while on-boarding remotely at UCF, so please bear with me.

Both NA predictors and offset() should work on rsf.fit(), but when using rsf.select() the latter will be preferred going forward for when predictors are not used in certain candidate models.

Best,
Chris

> > > > > > rsf.select() with verbose=TRUE returns the list of candidate models, and you can run summary() on any model in that list to see their parameter estimates, with the first model being the selected model.
> > > > > > In general, you do not want to feed non-selected models into mean() because unsupported features can cause numerical errors in the covariance matrix, and the covariance matrix is used in the meta-analysis weights. Unsupported features also aren't really going to be contributing very much information to the population estimates, anyhow.
> > > > > > mean() can handle different individuals having different selected parameters.
> > > > > > As a simple rule I would use rsf.select() before mean(), but the second model here probably wouldn't hurt anything because its within an AIC/parameter.
> > > > > > I can add an argument to drop NA location fixes - I'll add that to the to-do list.
> > > > > > Regarding the formula error, do you have the stats package loaded? Maybe try stats::offset(). I'll look into my code - I probably have set the formula environment incorrectly.
> > > > > > Yes, in any regression context, a categorical variable with N categories is expanded into N-1 indicator variables with N-1 regression parameters. Therefore, you might consider more parsimonious candidate models where some of those categories are combined in a reasonable way, and rsf.select() will not do this for you.
> > > > > > Yes, that is the approximate correction for the autocorrelation - using the autocorrelated Gaussian effective sample size rather than the nominal sample size: https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/2041-210X.14025
> > > > > > i. In any regression context, N categories is expanded into N-1 indicator variables that are relative to the reference category, which must be sampled. Here your predictors are 0 relative to 4, 1 relative to 4, 2 relative to 4, and 3 relative to 4. You can only ever estimate a categorical effect relative to a different category (or some combination thereof).
> > > > > > ii. If you have finely sampled raster data and aren't using a non-stationary model, then it should be faster to use Riemann.
> > > > > > iii. level.UD is only used for conventional non-integrated analyses, which is not recommended.
> > > > > > iv. With Monte-Carlo integration, you might adjust error for computational speed when setting up an analysis, otherwise you probably wouldn't touch those in normal use.
> > > > > > Yes and yes, but its better to use model selection to help tease out the significant parameters as unsupported parameters can potentially corrupt the covariance matrix estimate with numerical error.
> > > > > > The model-fit summary contains Gaussian area estimates and Gaussian RMS speed estimates. The akde() and speed() estimates are non-parametric: https://ctmm-initiative.github.io/ctmm/reference/summary.ctmm.html

messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris,

I have been trying to use the rsf.fit function for American kestrel GPS data, and have received an error producing the message: "missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed". I am following the rsf.fit vignette in ctmm learn using my data.

I was able to run the "TEST" line with the simplified rsf.fit without error:

TEST <- rsf.fit(cliftonKestrelTel[[i]],cliftonAKDES[[i]],R=list(habitat=cliftonEnvData))

However, when I ran the chunk below with the Riemann integrator I was receiving the following message:

RSF <- list()

for(i in 1:length(cliftonKestrelTel))

{

  RSF[[i]] <- rsf.fit(cliftonKestrelTel[[i]],cliftonAKDES[[i]],R=list(habitat=cliftonEnvData),integrator="Riemann",trace=2)

}

"Error in if (max(abs(c(diff(dX)/mid(dX), diff(dY)/mid(dY), diff(Xo)/mid(Xo), : missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed."

After reading other conversations in this group about similar errors, I updated ctmm through Github using devtools::install_github("ctmm-initiative/ctmm", force=TRUE, lib='myFolder'). After this, I am still receiving the same error message when using rsf.fit with the Riemann integrator. Do you know if this may be an issue on my end, or a bug within rsf.fit?

Thank you in advance for your time!

Best,
Megan

messages.subject: comparing AKDE's with considerably different numbers of locations
messages.subject_clean: comparing AKDE's with considerably different numbers of locations
messages.body_plain:
Good afternoon,

I have AKDE 95% and core homeranges based on birds with 4-6 locations a day, and I have homeranges from birds that have 30-120+ locations a day. Can I compare AKDE homeranges (95% and core) with that sort of GPS frequency disparity or would that be an inappropriate comparison to make due to the extreme difference in number of points each day?

Homeranges were calculated using methods in Buttler et al 2022, see below.

Butler, M.J., D.R. Stewart, G.M. Harris, M.T. Bidwell, and A.T. Pearse. 2022. Space use and site fidelity of wintering whooping cranes on the Texas Gulf Coast. Journal of Wildlife Management: e22226.

“We used the continuous‐time movement modeling (ctmm version 0.6.1) package for Program R version 4.0.5 (Fleming and Calabrese 2020, R CoreTeam 2021) to select and fit continuous‐time stochastic process models of movement and to estimate a home range using autocorrelated kernel density estimation (AKDE; Fleming et al. 2015, Calabrese et al. 2016, Fleming and Calabrese 2017). Traditional kernel density estimates (Worton 1989) do not allow for autocorrelated location data. Fleming et al. (2015) fully generalized the kernel density estimate to properly account for autocorrelation among locations in the ADKE. Once whooping cranes arrive on the wintering grounds, movements prior to settling into winter home ranges can be substantial and occur over several weeks. Therefore, we plotted locations, variograms, and outliers to determine an individual's movements and deleted GPS locations that were collected prior to a crane settling into its winter home range and outliers. Variograms plot the semi‐variance of locations as functions of the time lag between locations (Calabrese et al.  2016). Examination of the variogram reveals when individuals settle into a home range (i.e., variogram reaches an asymptote) and shows shifts in space use prior to settling into the home range (Calabrese et al. 2016). We indexed uncertainty in our location data with a categorical variable for fix quality (Pearse et al. 2020a). We used locations and fix quality from test transmitters (Pearse et al. 2017) and transmitters on carcasses to calibrate errors associated with our GPS devices (Fleming et al. 2016). This analysis related location error with fix quality and provided average error for each fix quality category. We assigned calibrated errors to the location data based on fix quality. Once we identified locations associated with range residency by an individual, we followed the workflow of Calabrese et al. (2016) to select and fit a movement model.

Traditional kernel density estimates of home range are underestimated when applied to serially autocorrelated data (Fleming et al. 2015). Therefore, we estimated home range areas using 95% AKDE based on the best fitting model. For comparison with previous work, we also estimated 95% and 50% minimum convex polygon (MCP) home ranges using the Program R package adehabitatHR version 0.4.19 (Calenge 2006).

For some individuals, location plots and abrupt changes on variograms suggested that some animals resided (were range resident) in multiple, distinct areas during a winter. In those situations, we fit different movement models to each period and estimated separate AKDEs and MCPs. If an individual had multiple home ranges within an overwintering period, we summed those home range areas for total winter home range area.

An animal's core home range is defined as the area of most concentrated use (Samuel et al. 1985, Seaman and Powell 1990). Often, the 50% isopleth of the kernel density is assumed as an appropriate core area, but differences in animal behavior or different distributions of resources within a home range can change intensity of space use across the home range (Vander Wal and Rodgers 2012). Therefore, we used an objective technique to determine the core isopleth of each home range instead of assuming 50% (Vander Wal and Rodgers 2012). To estimate the core isopleth and the core area of the AKDE home range for each individual, we determined the isopleth of the kernel density in which proportional use of the home range is equal to the predicted probability of use (Vander Wal and Rodgers 2012). Using nonlinear least‐squares (nls) regression in R, we regressed the proportional AKDE home range area as an exponential function of predicted probability of use (isopleth) for each home range. Isopleths used in this analysis were 10% to 90% in 10% increments, 95%, and 99%. The proportional area that each isopleth contained was based on the area of the 99% isopleth. We estimated the core area isopleth by setting the first derivative of the fitted nls model to one and solving for the isopleth value (Vander Wal and Rodgers 2012). If an individual had multiple home ranges within an overwintering period, we averaged core area isopleths for one estimate per bird per year.”

Thank you,

Carter G. Crouch, Ph.D.

Director of Gulf Coast Programs

Mobile: 940-704-6008

International Crane Foundation
802 Airport Rd. Suite 1 (physical address)

1919 Hwy 35 N, #610 (mailing address)

Rockport, TX 78382 USA

Hi Carter,

Yes, absolutely. This is the advantage of basing everything on a selected continuous-time stochastic process. You may find that the selected model for the finer-scale data is different than that of the coarse-scale data. This is appropriate and what makes the distribution estimates comparable (because they don't have that sampling dependent bias from assuming the same autocorrelation structure or lack of autocorrelation).

Best,
Chris

Hi Chris,

Thanks for the last message!

Since we last spoke I have been trying to find more information on the GPS device and if any calibration data and information on the error structure exists. We used the AWT GPS/UHF/VHF collars for the dogs. The habitat was mostly open (farm/grasslands) and human-built areas. I spoke to the AWT Technical Team and they suggested a standard error of 10-20 m. I definitely think 40-52 meter location error does not make sense for my data.

When I used a prior of 10 or 20 meters, the home range estimate (in hectares) was coming to almost half of what I received when I calculated it without a prior. I have attached home range estimates using different priors (5, 10, 20, and no prior) in the pdf.

You said I could enforce a stronger prior, what would that be? And is that safe?

This is what I used when I was simultaneously fitting with uncalibrated data. Does it make sense or am I missing something?
summary(uere(d7.hd1)) #default 10m error for GPS data
#Assigning 20-meter RMS UERE
uere(d7.hd1)<-c(20)
UERE<-uere(d7.hd1)
UERE$DOF
summary(UERE)
#D0F set to a smaller value to give plausible credible intervals
UERE$DOF[]<-2 summary(UERE)
#Assigning the prior to the data
uere(d7.hd1)<-UERE

# Calculate an automated model guesstimate: (with calibrated data)
d7hd1.GUESS <- ctmm.guess(d7.hd1, CTMM = ctmm(error= TRUE),interactive = FALSE)
# Automated model selection, starting from GUESS:
d7hd1.FIT <- ctmm.select(d7.hd1, d7hd1.GUESS, trace= TRUE, cores= 2)

Thanks once again,
Soham Mehta

messages.body_plain:
Hi Soham,

You can make the prior more informative by increasing the 'DOF' parameter. For instance:

data(buffalo)
UERE <- uere(buffalo)
UERE$UERE[,'horizontal'] <- 15
UERE$DOF[,'horizontal'] <- 8.5
summary(UERE)
uere(buffalo) <- UERE

This gives you an approximately 10-20 meter 95% credible interval for the prior, though that is not the same thing as a 10-20 meter 95% prediction interval.

Best,
Chris

messages.subject: Re: Optimal Weighing
messages.body_plain:
Hi Soham,

The 10-20 credible interval is the uncertainty for the root-mean-square (RMS) location error (a parameter of the error distribution) and not the prediction intervals of the posterior distribution (the range of errors that you tend to see).

If you had to, you could fix the RMS UERE (infinite DOF) and then report the sensitivity, most simply by running at 10 meters and 20 meters.

Best,
Chris

> > > > > > > > Yes, in any regression context, a categorical variable with N categories is expanded into N-1 indicator variables with N-1 regression parameters. Here your predictors are 0 relative to 4, 1 relative to 4, 2 relative to 4, and 3 relative to 4. You can only ever estimate a categorical effect relative to a different category (or some combination thereof).
> > > > > > > > ii. If you have finely sampled raster data and aren't using a non-stationary model, then it should be faster to use Riemann.

> > > > > > > > > > > > - Calculate population level/study area RSF parameter estimates using mean()
> > > > > > > > > > > >

Any idea when you might get a chance to build in the ignore NA functionality into rsf.fit()?

What type of standardization does rsf.fit() employ? Is it z-score i.e., (observed value - population mean) /  SD? Regards,
Luke.

> > > > > > > > > Yes, in any regression context, a categorical variable with N categories is expanded into N-1 indicator variables with N-1 regression parameters. Therefore, you might consider more parsimonious candidate models where some of those categories are combined in a reasonable way, and rsf.select() will not do this for you.
> > > > > > > > > Yes, that is the approximate correction for the autocorrelation - using the autocorrelated Gaussian effective sample size rather than the nominal sample size: https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/2041-210X.14025
> > > > > > > > > i. In any regression context, N categories is expanded into N-1 indicator variables that are relative to the reference category, which must be sampled. Here your predictors are 0 relative to 4, 1 relative to 4, 2 relative to 4, and 3 relative to 4. You can only ever estimate a categorical effect relative to a different category (or some combination thereof).
> > > > > > > > > ii. If you have finely sampled raster data and aren't using a non-stationary model, then it should be faster to use Riemann.
> > > > > > > > > iii. level.UD is only used for conventional non-integrated analyses, which is not recommended.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Luke,

I'll have it in the next week or two - I'm just extremely busy at this moment and prioritizing bug fixes over feature requests.

The standardization in rsf.fit() is the simplistic z-score, which is disabled when you use a formula, because something like square terms or interaction terms means that the code doesn't know how to back-transform the betas. If using those terms, it is up to you to standardize/normalize your predictors before rsf.fit() and I would suggest something simple, like if one predictor is aspect angles between 0 and 90 degrees by definition, then dividing by 90 will give values that have a mean and standard deviation not too different from 1, which is what you want. What you don't want to do is to standardize/normalize the predictors differently on different datasets if you aren't going to back-transform the corresponding betas.

Best,
Chris

messages.body_plain:
Hi Soham,

I mean running the analysis with exactly 10-meter and then 20-meter RMS UERE and noting the difference or sensitivity to that choice. An assignment of uere(DATA) <- 10 will fix the RMS UERE to 10 meters exactly.

A higher DOF also makes sense, but then you also question the sensitivity to the RMS UERE (there centered on 15 meters).

Best,
Chris

Hi Chris,

Thanks for your help! Sorry for asking so many questions, I am new to this topic.

1. I ran the analysis as you suggested. I got an estimate of 7.872677 hectares at 10-meter RMS UERE and 7.254819 hectares at 20-meters. I believe that the difference is not huge, what do you suggest I do in this case? Attached a screenshot.
2. Also, on what basis would you decide the DOF?
3. Lastly, what would you recommend I do as I go ahead with my analysis? I know the GPS device's standard error is 10-20 meters. Is it safe to run my analysis at a 15 meter RMS UERE with a higher DOF (for e.g. 10 instead of 8.5; I got a huge difference when I ran both) or run it at 15 meters exact?

Appreciate it,
Soham

Hi Soham,

That's what I would report.
Bayesian priors are subjective. The DOF is how many data points your opinion is worth.
The 10 and 20-meter fixed RMS UEREs are your most reasonable result so far. I would report that, because it tells you the sensitivity to an assumed range of parameters. Using a 15-meter RMS UERE with a high DOF is relatively opaque.
Best,
Chris

> > > > > > > > > > > Yes, that is the approximate correction for the autocorrelation - using the autocorrelated Gaussian effective sample size rather than the nominal sample size: https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/2041-210X.14025
> > > > > > > > > > > i. In any regression context, N categories is expanded into N-1 indicator variables that are relative to the reference category, which must be sampled. > > > > > > > > > > > ii. If you have finely sampled raster data and aren't using a non-stationary model, then it should be faster to use Riemann.
> > > > > > > > > > > iii. level.UD is only used for conventional non-integrated analyses, which is not recommended.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Soham,

A fixed value is the same as an infinite DOF. The problem that you were running into with small DOFs was that the updated posterior was like something you would only see underneath very dense canopy and brush. The higher the DOF, the less the value will be updated and infinite DOF will not update.

So, in your  case, I would run a plausible range of fixed values and report the sensitivity. One way to do that would be a fixed 15-meter error and then to report how +/-5 meters of error changes your results.

Best,
Chris

Chris

The problem that you were running into with small DOFs was that the updated posterior was like something you would only see underneath very dense canopy and brush. messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I working on fitting an iRSF with an interaction between a categorical raster (land cover) and a time dependent covariate (sunlight from annotate) and when I run  rsf.select I encounter the same error as Mike, Error in NEW[[i]] : attempt to select less than one element in get1index. It seems that I have no trouble fitting iRSF's with interactions between continuous raster covariates and etiher continuous or categorical time dependent covariates. Anyways, I haven't been able to solve it yet so I was wondering if you Mike or Chris (or anyone) have found a solution and might be able to help me out? See below for my session info and a reproducible example.

Cheers,
Chad

###### Reprex:
require(sf)
require(terra)
require(tidyverse)
require(ctmm)

data(buffalo)
DATA <- buffalo$Cilla
GUESS <- ctmm.guess(DATA, interactive = FALSE)
FIT <- ctmm.select(DATA, GUESS)
UD <- akde(DATA, FIT)

tst_r <- UD %>%
  as.sf %>%
  st_buffer(10000) %>%
  st_bbox %>%
  st_as_sfc %>%
  st_as_sf %>%
  rast(resolution = 100)

nr <- nrow(tst_r)
nc <- ncol(tst_r)

values(tst_r) <- round(runif(nr * nc, 0, 7))
tst_r <- raster::raster(tst_r)
tst_r_c <- raster::as.factor(tst_r)
r_list <- list(tst_r = tst_r)
r_list_c <- list(tst_r_c = tst_r_c)

DATA <- annotate(DATA)

RSF_c <- rsf.select(DATA, UD, R = r_list_c, formula = ~ tst_r_c + tst_r_c:sunlight)
RSF <- rsf.select(DATA, UD, R = r_list, formula = ~tst_r + tst_r:sunlight)
###### END

Hi Chris,

Sorry, me again!

When including interaction terms in rsf.select():
1. If the best fit model selected contains an interaction term, will the corresponding main effects (i.e. contributing predictors) be automatically/always included in that model as well? My internet reading suggests that main effects should typically be included in a model where the corresponding interaction term is included.

RSF <- rsf.select(DATA, UD, R = r_list, formula = ~tst_r + tst_r:sunlight)
###### END

messages.body_plain:
Hi Luke,

rsf.select() will not enforce that model structure, but you can have verbose=TRUE and then select from only candidate models that you believe have the appropriate biological structure. However, I could imagine a selection like ~tree_cover:day_time that would not necessarily have the main effect of tree_cover, and day_time would never be a main effect in a spatial point-process model (rsf.fit() should turn that off if you try it).
You would want to structure the models so that you are selecting among a null model, a model with an overall main effect, and a model with an overall main effect + an interaction that is on-average zero and provides extra detail to the main-effect model. If you don't or can't structure the models so that the interpretations are the same as you add predictors, then you could very well end up averaging coefficients nonsensically.
Yes, but I would recommend a simple rescaling of the predictors so that you never worry about back transforming.
For the moment, you need to remove those points at the beginning of the analysis, but I'm going to try to have an argument for that in rsf.fit() within a couple of weeks. But removing those data points is not the same as making that area unavailable in the RSF model.
Best,
Chris

Given I ultimately want to calculate mean coefficient estimates from all RSF outputs for study population, can coefficients for main effects in best fit models that DO and DO NOT contain interaction terms be considered the same and therefore have their mean calculated? If this is the case, I may be best served by not including any interaction terms given I want to calculate coefficient mean across all individuals for each parameter/predictor. Otherwise I would have to calculate the mean coefficient for predictors/parameters where an interaction term WAS NOT included in the best fit model, and a separate mean coefficient for the same predictors/parameters where an interaction term WAS included in the best fit model. What you don't want to do is to standardize/normalize the predictors differently on different datasets if you aren't going to back-transform the corresponding betas.

Here your predictors are 0 relative to 4, 1 relative to 4, 2 relative to 4, and 3 relative to 4. > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > We are wanting to assess the influence of study area/population level factors (including the presence or not of wolves, bears, and/or puma hunting by humans) on the selection of critical habitat characteristics (specifically feeding/kill sites and bed sites) of pumas. We have GPS collar data for multiple pumas across multiple study areas in both North and South America and multiple kill and bed sites for each puma. Study areas are exposed to differing combinations of external factors (i.e. wolves, bears, humans). So, we are more interested in what is happening at a population level per study area rather than at the individual puma level. I understand we can derive population level parameters from RSFs by placing individual estimates in a list and calculating mean().
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Given the presence of bears and hunting are seasonal, it would seem prudent that we create seasonal RSFs. Below is a potential workflow:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Habitat selection per seasonal home range:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > - Split all movement/location data for each puma according to season (e.g. winter vs summer)
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > - Calculate akdes per season
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > - Create separate RSFs for winter and summer for each individual, using seasonal akdes and location data (I think NDVI will be the only time dependent variable being used in the RSFS, so we should use mean summer NDVI for summer RSF, and use mean winter NDVI for winter RSF)
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > - Calculate population level/study area RSF parameter estimates using mean()
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Habitat selection for bed and kill sites per season:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > - Split kill and bed sites by season
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > - Create separate RSFs for winter and summer for each individual for kill sites and bed sites, using seasonal akdes and kill and bed site locations
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > - Calculate population level/study area RSF parameter estimates using mean()
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Hence, I was thinking of creating the following 9 RSFs per individual before deriving population level parameter estimates:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 1. all locations
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 2. all kill sites
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 3. all bed sites
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 4. winter only locations
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 5. winter only kill sites
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 6. winter only bed sites
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 7. summer locations
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 8. summer kill sites
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 9. summer bed sites
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > Questions:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 1. Is the above workflow appropriate to account for potential seasonal differences in habitat selection by pumas?
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 2. If an individual puma is monitored across multiple years and therefore multiple seasons (e.g. 3 winters and 2 summers), do I need to calculate individual akdes per season per year (i.e. 1st akde for winter 1, 2nd akde for winter 2, 3rd akde for winter 3, etc) and then calculate the mean akde before RSF fitting, to account for the large gap in time between seasons and the influence on range-residency assumption? Or can I just create a single seasonal akde from the beginning, despite a large time gap between the same season across multiple years?
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > 3. If I want to assess seasonal habitat selection, do I need to first create a seasonal akde (i.e. Winter kill site selection should only be assessed relative to winter akde, not the entire akde across all seasons)?

messages.body_plain:
Thanks Chris,

Just to clarify a couple of things you mentioned in your previous response:

1. "You would want to structure the models so that you are selecting among a null model, a model with an overall main effect, and a model with an overall main effect + an interaction that is on-average zero and provides extra detail to the main-effect model. If you don't or can't structure the models so that the interpretations are the same as you add predictors, then you could very well end up averaging coefficients nonsensically."

I was originally thinking I could just throw all my predictor rasters into rsf.select(), extract the best performing model for each individual puma based on AICc, then calculate population level mean parameter coefficients for each parameter that appears in the best performing model per puma by using mean() function. However, based on what you said it might not be this simple.

a) Based on your comment above, when determining whether it is appropriate to calculate the mean() of parameter coefficients across best fit models for each puma, would below be a suitable workflow?
     i) Run rsf.select()/rsf.fit() on all predictors and review AICc of all models using verbose = TRUE
     ii) Review the model outputs and ensure that the best fit model has significantly more support than the NULL model (i.e. NULL model is >2 delta AICc) (Or does this not matter if calculating mean() parameter coefficients across the population? Would I just include the best fit model in the mean() calculations even if the NULL is <2 delta AICc?)
     iii) Ensure that coefficients for the main effects/predictors/parameters of the best fit model remain consistent/similar across all other models (Or just models that are <2 delta AICc?)
     iii) If the best fit model doesn't contain any interaction terms, then ensure that the confidence interval for the interaction term coefficient crosses zero in other models (e.g. ~tree_cover+ tree_cover:distance_to_road    -   $CI  tree_cover:distance_to_road   low =  -2.1734673    est = 0.4598783    high = 3.093224). (Or should this just be done for models <2 delta AICc that contain interaction terms composed of the main effects from the best fit model?)
     iv) If the best fit model contains main effects and interaction term/s then ensure the coefficients of main effects remain consistent/similar across other models (all models?)
     v) If the best fit model contains only an interaction term, then review other models <2 delta AICc and if there is a model containing the main effects and interaction terms of the best fit model and the main effects do not cross zero, then select model with main effects and interaction term (e.g. ~ A + B + A:B  or  ~ A + A:B  or  ~B + A:B) (Would this be appropriate?)
     vi) If these conditions are met then use the model as part of mean() parameter estimate calculations, if not, remove the model

b) If for example I want to assess the selection of ~aspect + tree_cover + distance_to_water + distance_to_road + terrain_roughness + tree_cover:distance_to_road, using rsf.select(), and the best fit RSF models for multiple pumas were per below, and the parameter/model selection meet the criteria outlined above, is it appropriate to then calculate the population mean() parameter coefficients across all the non NULL models?
Puma 1 = ~ tree_cover + terrain_roughness
Puma 2 =  ~ tree_cover + distance_to_road
Puma 3 = ~ distance_to_water + tree_cover:distance_to_road
Puma 4 = ~ tree_cover + tree_cover:distance_to_road
Puma 5 = ~  tree_cover:distance_to_road
Puma 6 = ~ distance_to_road
Puma 7 = ~ tree_cover
Puma 8 = NULL model

2. "For the moment, you need to remove those points at the beginning of the analysis, but I'm going to try to have an argument for that in rsf.fit() within a couple of weeks. But removing those data points is not the same as making that area unavailable in the RSF model."

Apologies if I wasn't clear in my previous question. I have removed puma locations that fall within water before calculating UDs through akde(), and I have made areas of water "no data" in the predictor rasters, and these areas of water are represented by value of 0 in the offset_raster. Given this, I assume the use of an offset_raster in the rsf.select() formula will be redundant because I have already made the areas of water "no data" in the predictor rasters (i.e. 0 values in offset_raster). Is this correct or am I misinterpreting what offset() does?

3. Previously you said: "The dataset that goes into rsf.fit() needs to be the same as what went into the akde() weights, or the weights and data points will not match."

I was hoping to use rsf.select()/rsf.fit() to also assess habitat selection of puma kill sites and bed sites relative to available habitat across their entire home range (i.e. their UD), but we typically only have 10 to 30 kill or bed site locations per puma. Is this going to be a problem when the UD dataset is based on hundreds or thousands of locations (and weights), and the kill or bed site location data only contains 10 to 30 locations (i.e. the UD and kill or bed site datasets don't match)? If this is a problem, is there anyway around this using ctmm?

Many thanks,
Luke

> Hi Luke,
>
> rsf.select() will not enforce that model structure, but you can have verbose=TRUE and then select from only candidate models that you believe have the appropriate biological structure. However, I could imagine a selection like ~tree_cover:day_time that would not necessarily have the main effect of tree_cover, and day_time would never be a main effect in a spatial point-process model (rsf.fit() should turn that off if you try it).
> You would want to structure the models so that you are selecting among a null model, a model with an overall main effect, and a model with an overall main effect + an interaction that is on-average zero and provides extra detail to the main-effect model. If you don't or can't structure the models so that the interpretations are the same as you add predictors, then you could very well end up averaging coefficients nonsensically.

> require(sf)

>
> data(buffalo)

>

messages.body_plain:
Hi Luke,

1.a) You want to include selected models to avoid ill-conditioned covariance matrices, but that selection needn't be strong. You don't need to test for significance.

mean() allows for missing predictors. You just need to structure the interactions consistently. For instance:

~ tree_cover + tree_cover:day

could equivalently be modeled as

~tree_cover + tree_cover:night

or

~tree_cover:day + tree_cover:night

but you want a consistent choice here that also makes sense for model selection to first be able to select the largest overall effect and then be able to refine that with additional terms.

1.b) Looks fine to me.
2.) With the null model, NA predictor values aren't ensured to work when the predictors aren't being used, whereas offset()will be maintained going forward.
3.) I'm not sure what you are asking here. How do you plan to make this comparison?

Best,
Chris

On Thursday, August 24, 2023 at 1:47:52 AM UTC-4 lukedaniel...@googlemail.com wrote:
> Thanks Chris,
>
> Just to clarify a couple of things you mentioned in your previous response:
>
> 1. "You would want to structure the models so that you are selecting among a null model, a model with an overall main effect, and a model with an overall main effect + an interaction that is on-average zero and provides extra detail to the main-effect model. If you don't or can't structure the models so that the interpretations are the same as you add predictors, then you could very well end up averaging coefficients nonsensically."
>
> I was originally thinking I could just throw all my predictor rasters into rsf.select(), extract the best performing model for each individual puma based on AICc, then calculate population level mean parameter coefficients for each parameter that appears in the best performing model per puma by using mean() function. However, based on what you said it might not be this simple.
>
> a) Based on your comment above, when determining whether it is appropriate to calculate the mean() of parameter coefficients across best fit models for each puma, would below be a suitable workflow?
>      i) Run rsf.select()/rsf.fit() on all predictors and review AICc of all models using verbose = TRUE
>      ii) Review the model outputs and ensure that the best fit model has significantly more support than the NULL model (i.e. NULL model is >2 delta AICc) (Or does this not matter if calculating mean() parameter coefficients across the population? Would I just include the best fit model in the mean() calculations even if the NULL is <2 delta AICc?)
>      iii) Ensure that coefficients for the main effects/predictors/parameters of the best fit model remain consistent/similar across all other models (Or just models that are <2 delta AICc?)
>      iii) If the best fit model doesn't contain any interaction terms, then ensure that the confidence interval for the interaction term coefficient crosses zero in other models (e.g. ~tree_cover+ tree_cover:distance_to_road    -   $CI  tree_cover:distance_to_road   low =  -2.1734673    est = 0.4598783    high = 3.093224). (Or should this just be done for models <2 delta AICc that contain interaction terms composed of the main effects from the best fit model?)
>      iv) If the best fit model contains main effects and interaction term/s then ensure the coefficients of main effects remain consistent/similar across other models (all models?)
>      v) If the best fit model contains only an interaction term, then review other models <2 delta AICc and if there is a model containing the main effects and interaction terms of the best fit model and the main effects do not cross zero, then select model with main effects and interaction term (e.g. ~ A + B + A:B  or  ~ A + A:B  or  ~B + A:B) (Would this be appropriate?)
>      vi) If these conditions are met then use the model as part of mean() parameter estimate calculations, if not, remove the model
>
> b) If for example I want to assess the selection of ~aspect + tree_cover + distance_to_water + distance_to_road + terrain_roughness + tree_cover:distance_to_road, using rsf.select(), and the best fit RSF models for multiple pumas were per below, and the parameter/model selection meet the criteria outlined above, is it appropriate to then calculate the population mean() parameter coefficients across all the non NULL models?
> Puma 1 = ~ tree_cover + terrain_roughness
> Puma 2 =  ~ tree_cover + distance_to_road
> Puma 3 = ~ distance_to_water + tree_cover:distance_to_road
> Puma 4 = ~ tree_cover + tree_cover:distance_to_road
> Puma 5 = ~  tree_cover:distance_to_road
> Puma 6 = ~ distance_to_road
> Puma 7 = ~ tree_cover
> Puma 8 = NULL model
>
>
>
> 2. "For the moment, you need to remove those points at the beginning of the analysis, but I'm going to try to have an argument for that in rsf.fit() within a couple of weeks. But removing those data points is not the same as making that area unavailable in the RSF model."
>
> Apologies if I wasn't clear in my previous question. I have removed puma locations that fall within water before calculating UDs through akde(), and I have made areas of water "no data" in the predictor rasters, and these areas of water are represented by value of 0 in the offset_raster. Given this, I assume the use of an offset_raster in the rsf.select() formula will be redundant because I have already made the areas of water "no data" in the predictor rasters (i.e. 0 values in offset_raster). Is this correct or am I misinterpreting what offset() does?
>
>
>
> 3. Previously you said: "The dataset that goes into rsf.fit() needs to be the same as what went into the akde() weights, or the weights and data points will not match."
>
> I was hoping to use rsf.select()/rsf.fit() to also assess habitat selection of puma kill sites and bed sites relative to available habitat across their entire home range (i.e. their UD), but we typically only have 10 to 30 kill or bed site locations per puma. If this is a problem, is there anyway around this using ctmm?

> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > i. In any regression context, N categories is expanded into N-1 indicator variables that are relative to the reference category, which must be sampled. Here your predictors are 0 relative to 4, 1 relative to 4, 2 relative to 4, and 3 relative to 4. You can only ever estimate a categorical effect relative to a different category (or some combination thereof).
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > ii. If you have finely sampled raster data and aren't using a non-stationary model, then it should be faster to use Riemann.

> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > iv. With Monte-Carlo integration, you might adjust error for computational speed when setting up an analysis, otherwise you probably wouldn't touch those in normal use.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris,

Thanks for the reply! :)

Re. my previous question:

3. Previously you said: "The dataset that goes into rsf.fit() needs to be the same as what went into the akde() weights, or the weights and data points will not match."

I want to create RSFs to assess habitat selection for kill sites and bed sites for each puma (for which we have these data) and determine if habitat attributes associated with kills sites and bed sites differ from each other, and if they also differ from general habitat use use across the entire home range (based on all locations from movement data). I also want to look at potential differences between seasonal habitat selection, hence I was planning on building the following 9 RSFs per individual and then calculating mean() parameter coefficients from each (not all individuals have kill site and bed site data though, so the number of individuals contributing to each mean() population level parameter coefficient will vary).

RSFs per individual:

1. all locations
2. all kill sites
3. all bed sites
4. winter only locations
5. winter only kill sites
6. winter only bed sites
7. summer locations
8. summer kill sites
9. summer bed sites

Creating RSFs for 1, 4 & 9 above seems to be fine because the number of locations/weights informing the UD created by akde() will remain the same for rsf.select()/rsf.fit(), because I will split the data based on season and create seasonal UDs and run seasonal RSFs accordingly.

In previous correspondence with Jesse, I had asked:

"Is rsf.fit appropriate for fitting RSFs to bed and kill sites for individual pumas when we might only have 5-40 bed or kill sites per individual?"

and he said

"Yes. The movement model selected will likely be IID, but that's fine--just means adjusting for autocorrelation isn't important"

However, given kill sites and bed sites represent a very limited number of locations per individual, and this number obviously doesn't represent the same number of locations/weights informing the UD/home range for each individual, it appears I can't use rsf.select()/rsf.fit() to create RSFs for kill and bed sites per puma because the accompanying UD will be based on hundreds or thousands of locations and the kill or bed site locations represent only a handful of these, e.g. 10 - 30 locations in some cases.

Does this mean that there is no way of running the kill and bed site part of my analysis in ctmm, and instead I would need to use a more traditional RSF approach of sampling a random number of available but "unused" locations per kill or bed site location within an individual's home range to determine habitat selection and parameter coefficients associated with kill and bed sites? Or is there a way of using an individual's UD in rsf.select()/rsf.fit() but suppressing the need for the number of weights to match the number of locations (i.e. kill sites or bed sites), for which we want to determine parameter coefficients?

Hope that makes sense now.

Cheers,
Luke

> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > i. In any regression context, N categories is expanded into N-1 indicator variables that are relative to the reference category, which must be sampled. Here your predictors are 0 relative to 4, 1 relative to 4, 2 relative to 4, and 3 relative to 4. You can only ever estimate a categorical effect relative to a different category (or some combination thereof).
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > ii. If you have finely sampled raster data and aren't using a non-stationary model, then it should be faster to use Riemann.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > > > iii. level.UD is only used for conventional non-integrated analyses, which is not recommended.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Soham,

The two values provided by the manufacturer are about the same (12.5 and 13.3 meters/HDOP). You just need to make sure that you have the HDOP values in your data when you import them, and that they are recognized by as.telemetry(), which you will see in the output object from names() or head(). Anything in Movebank format should work, but other formats will probably work too.

If your results aren't sensitive to a 10-20 meters/HDOP value then I would expect an even smaller difference with the tighter 12.5-13.3 meter/HDOP value provided by the manufacturer.

Best,
Chris
